title: Δῶρα καὶ βουλαί
about: Ajax tells the heralds that Hector, who began the challenge, should be the one to propose an end to it. Hector agrees that night is falling and suggests the two champions part with an exchange of gifts, so that men may say they fought in strife and parted in friendship. He gives Ajax a silver-studded sword and Ajax gives him a crimson belt. The Trojans welcome Hector back, and the Achaeans lead Ajax to Agamemnon, who sacrifices an ox to Zeus and honours him with long unbroken cuts of chine. Nestor then proposes burning the dead at dawn under one mound, with towers, gates and a ditch before the ships. In Troy, Antenor urges giving Helen and her goods back; Paris refuses Helen but offers the goods and more. Priam sends Idaeus to the Achaeans at dawn with that offer and a request for a truce to burn the dead.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: In answer Telamonian Ajax said to him:
sentences.n: Ajax answers Idaeus, the Trojan herald whose plea to stop for the night ended the previous part. τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is the standing reply-formula, ‘answering him, he addressed’: ἀπαμειβόμενος is a participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, and προσέφη a past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. Τελαμώνιος Αἴας is ‘Telamonian Ajax’, the adjective (‘of Telamon’) telling him from the other Ajax. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: Ἰδαῖ’ Ἕκτορα ταῦτα κελεύετε μυθήσασθαι·
sentences.l: “Idaeus, bid Hector to speak these things;
sentences.i: “Idaeus, bid Hector say these things;
sentences.n: Ajax hands the proposal back to Hector. Ἰδαῖ’ is the vocative Ἰδαῖε with its last vowel elided. κελεύετε is plural, ‘you bid’, though only Idaeus is named; the plural may take in the other herald, Talthybius, who stood beside him. ταῦτα ‘these things’ is what Idaeus has just proposed, a stop to the fighting for the night. μυθήσασθαι is the aorist infinitive of μυθέομαι ‘say, speak out’. Ajax’s speech begins.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς γὰρ χάρμῃ προκαλέσσατο πάντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.l: for he himself, in the joy of battle, challenged all the best.
sentences.i: for it was he himself who challenged all the best men, in the joy of battle.
sentences.n: His reason: the challenge was Hector’s own. αὐτὸς γάρ ‘for he himself’ puts the weight on Hector. χάρμῃ is the dative of χάρμη ‘joy of battle’, and says in what spirit he acted. προκαλέσσατο is the aorist middle of προκαλέω ‘call forth, challenge’, and πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best men’ are the champions Hector called out earlier in this book.

sentences.t: ἀρχέτω·
sentences.l: let him begin;
sentences.i: let him begin;
sentences.n: ἀρχέτω is the third-person imperative of ἄρχω, here ‘let him begin’ (elsewhere the verb is ‘lead’): Hector made the challenge, so Hector is to open the talk of stopping. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ μάλα πείσομαι ᾗ περ ἂν οὗτος.
sentences.l: but I shall obey very readily in whatever way this man (begins).”
sentences.i: and I shall readily obey, in whatever way he begins.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ sets Ajax’s own part against Hector’s. πείσομαι is the future of πείθομαι ‘obey’ (not the future of πάσχω ‘suffer’, which has the same form), and μάλα is ‘very much, readily’. ᾗ περ ἂν οὗτος is ‘in whatever way this man (may begin)’: ᾗ is a relative adverb ‘in the way that’, περ strengthens it, and οὗτος points at Hector. The verb is left out and is understood from ἀρχέτω. Ajax’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Hector replies to Ajax. The line is a stock speech-introduction: αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks the second speaker, τὸν ‘him’ is Ajax, προσέειπε is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’, and μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ is ‘great Hector of the glancing helmet’, where κορυθαίολος joins κόρυς ‘helmet’ and αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν ἐπεί τοι δῶκε θεὸς μέγεθός τε βίην τε
καὶ πινυτήν, περὶ δ’ ἔγχει Ἀχαιῶν φέρτατός ἐσσι,
sentences.l:
“Ajax, since to you a god has given size and strength
and discernment, and with the spear you are by far the best of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: “Ajax, since a god has given you size and strength and discernment, and with the spear you are by far the best of the Achaeans,
sentences.n: Hector begins with praise, and the sentence runs on into the next unit. Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας, τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and δῶκε θεός is ‘a god gave’, with no god named. μέγεθος ‘size’, βίη ‘strength’ and πινυτή ‘discernment, good sense’ (a noun from the same root as πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’) are the three gifts. περὶ δ’ ἔγχει Ἀχαιῶν φέρτατός ἐσσι is ‘beyond others, with the spear, you are best of the Achaeans’: περί is an adverb, ἔγχει the dative ‘in the spear’, ἐσσί the epic ‘you are’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν παυσώμεσθα μάχης καὶ δηϊοτῆτος
σήμερον·
sentences.l:
now let us cease from battle and from fighting
today;
sentences.i: Now let us leave off battle and fighting for today;
sentences.n: Here is the proposal. νῦν μέν ‘now’ is answered by ὕστερον αὖτε ‘later again’ in the next unit. παυσώμεσθα is the first-person plural subjunctive middle of παύω, ‘let us stop’, with the genitives μάχης καὶ δηϊοτῆτος ‘from battle and fighting’ (δηϊοτής is the epic word for fighting). σήμερον ‘today’ makes it a stop for one day only. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 291.

sentences.t:
ὕστερον αὖτε μαχησόμεθ’ εἰς ὅ κε δαίμων
ἄμμε διακρίνῃ, δώῃ δ’ ἑτέροισί γε νίκην.
sentences.l:
Later in turn we shall fight, until a divinity
parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.
sentences.i: Later we shall fight again, until a divinity parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.
sentences.n: The fight is only put off. μαχησόμεθ’ is the future of μάχομαι ‘fight’, εἰς ὅ κε … διακρίνῃ ‘until … shall part’ takes κε and the subjunctive, and ἄμμε is the old form of ἡμᾶς ‘us’. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, ‘a divinity’. δώῃ is the epic subjunctive of δίδωμι, and ἑτέροισί γε νίκην is ‘victory to one side or the other’: ἕτερος picks one of two, here a party, and γε is a particle of emphasis. Priam’s message repeats these two lines at 377–378.

sentences.t: νὺξ δ’ ἤδη τελέθει·
sentences.l: and night is already here;
sentences.i: night is already here;
sentences.n: Hector gives the reason for stopping, in the words Idaeus used at the end of the previous part (7.282). τελέθει is the present of τελέθω ‘be, come to be’; with νύξ ‘night’ and ἤδη ‘already’ it says that night has now arrived. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἀγαθὸν καὶ νυκτὶ πιθέσθαι,
ὡς σύ τ’ ἐϋφρήνῃς πάντας παρὰ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιούς,
σούς τε μάλιστα ἔτας καὶ ἑταίρους, οἵ τοι ἔασιν·
sentences.i: it is good to yield to night as well, so that you may gladden all the Achaeans by the ships, and most of all your own kinsmen and companions, those who are yours;
sentences.n: Night is a reason to feast and rest. ἀγαθόν ‘good’ has ἐστί understood, and πιθέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of πείθω, ‘obey, yield to’, with νυκτί in the dative; the words repeat Idaeus’ last line. ὡς σύ τ’ ἐϋφρήνῃς is a purpose clause, ‘so that you may gladden’ (ἐϋφραίνω). ἔτας is the accusative plural of ἔτης ‘kinsman’, ἑταίρους ‘companions’, σούς ‘your own’, and οἵ τοι ἔασιν ‘who are yours’, with τοι for σοι and ἔασιν the epic ‘are’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ κατὰ ἄστυ μέγα Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
Τρῶας ἐϋφρανέω καὶ Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους,
αἵ τέ μοι εὐχόμεναι θεῖον δύσονται ἀγῶνα.
sentences.l:
but I, throughout the great town of lord Priam,
will gladden the Trojans and the Trojan women trailing-robed,
who, praying for me, will enter the divine gathering.
sentences.i: while I, throughout the great town of lord Priam, shall gladden the Trojans and the Trojan women with their trailing robes, who will go praying for me into the divine gathering.
sentences.n: Hector sets his own side against the Achaeans of the last unit: αὐτὰρ ἐγώ ‘but I’. ἄνακτος is ‘of the lord’, said of Priam, and ἐϋφρανέω is the epic future of ἐϋφραίνω, ‘I shall gladden’. Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους is the stock phrase ‘Trojan women with trailing robes’. In the last line αἵ is the feminine relative and εὐχόμεναι μοι ‘praying for me’; δύσονται is ‘will enter’, and ἀγών is ‘gathering’, made divine by θεῖον. The Greek does not say which gathering or place is meant, so the sense of the line is not certain.

sentences.t:
δῶρα δ’ ἄγ’ ἀλλήλοισι περικλυτὰ δώομεν ἄμφω,
ὄφρά τις ὧδ’ εἴπῃσιν Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε·
sentences.l:
But come, to one another very famous gifts let us give, both of us,
so that someone of the Achaeans and of the Trojans may say thus:
sentences.i: But come, let us both give each other very famous gifts, so that any man, Achaean or Trojan, may say:
sentences.n: Hector proposes an exchange of gifts and says what he wants men to say of it. δώομεν is a first-person plural subjunctive of δίδωμι with the short vowel, ‘let us give’; ἀλλήλοισι is ‘to one another’ and ἄμφω ‘both of us’. περικλυτά is ‘very famous’ (περι- ‘very’, κλυτός ‘famous’). ὄφρά τις … εἴπῃσιν is a purpose clause, ‘so that someone may say’, with an old form of the subjunctive; Ἀχαιῶν τε Τρώων τε says the speaker may come from either army, and ὧδε points ahead to the words of the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἠμὲν ἐμαρνάσθην ἔριδος πέρι θυμοβόροιο,
ἠδ’ αὖτ’ ἐν φιλότητι διέτμαγεν ἀρθμήσαντε.
sentences.l:
‘The two both fought over heart-devouring strife,
and again in friendship parted, joined as friends.’”
sentences.i: ‘These two fought in heart-devouring strife, and then parted again in friendship, joined as friends.’”
sentences.n: What the onlooker will say: ἠμέν … ἠδέ ‘both … and’. ἐμαρνάσθην is the dual imperfect of μάρναμαι ‘fight’, ‘the two fought’, with ἔριδος πέρι ‘over strife’ (πέρι follows its noun; ‘in strife’ in i) and θυμοβόροιο ‘heart-devouring’ (θυμός ‘heart’ + the root of βιβρώσκω ‘eat’). διέτμαγεν is the aorist passive of διατμήγω ‘cut apart, part’, a plural form that here serves for the two, as at 1.531; ἀρθμήσαντε is the dual aorist participle of ἀρθμέω ‘be joined in friendship’ (from ἀρθμός ‘bond’). Hector’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας δῶκε ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον
σὺν κολεῷ τε φέρων καὶ ἐϋτμήτῳ τελαμῶνι·
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, he gave the silver-studded sword,
bringing it with its sheath and well-cut strap;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and gave him the silver-studded sword, bringing it with its sheath and its well-cut strap;
sentences.n: Hector is the giver, though the line does not name him; it follows his speech. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is ‘so then, having spoken’. ξίφος ἀργυρόηλον is ‘the silver-studded sword’ (ἀργυρο- ‘silver’ + ἧλος ‘stud, nail’). σὺν κολεῷ is ‘with the sheath’, φέρων ‘bringing’, and ἐϋτμήτῳ τελαμῶνι ‘a well-cut strap’: the strap the sword hangs by (the same word is a shield-strap at 2.388). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: Αἴας δὲ ζωστῆρα δίδου φοίνικι φαεινόν.
sentences.l: and Ajax was giving a belt, shining with crimson.
sentences.i: and Ajax gave a belt shining with crimson.
sentences.n: Ajax gives in return. δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι without its augment (Attic ἐδίδου), ‘was giving’. ζωστήρ is a belt, φοίνικι φαεινόν ‘shining with crimson’: φοῖνιξ is the crimson dye, in the dative, and φαεινόν the accusative of φαεινός ‘shining’, agreeing with ζωστῆρα.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ διακρινθέντε ὃ μὲν μετὰ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν
ἤϊ’, ὃ δ’ ἐς Τρώων ὅμαδον κίε·
sentences.l:
And the two, having been parted, the one to the people of the Achaeans
went, the other to the uproar of the Trojans went;
sentences.i: The two parted, the one going to the people of the Achaeans, the other to the noisy crowd of the Trojans;
sentences.n: The two champions part. τὼ is the dual article ‘the two’, and διακρινθέντε the dual aorist passive participle of διακρίνω ‘part’ (the verb of ἄμμε διακρίνῃ above). ὃ μέν … ὃ δέ is ‘the one … the other’: the first is Ajax, who goes to the Achaeans, the second Hector, as the next lines show. ἤϊ’ is ἤϊε, the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and κίε the imperfect of κίω ‘go’. ὅμαδος is the din a crowd makes, and so the crowd. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 307.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ χάρησαν,
ὡς εἶδον ζωόν τε καὶ ἀρτεμέα προσιόντα,
Αἴαντος προφυγόντα μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἀάπτους·
sentences.i: and they were glad when they saw him alive and unharmed, coming toward them, having escaped the might of Ajax and his irresistible hands;
sentences.n: The Trojans welcome Hector back. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, and χάρησαν the aorist of χαίρω ‘rejoice’. ζωόν ‘alive’ and ἀρτεμέα ‘unharmed’ agree with the unnamed Hector, as do προσιόντα ‘coming near’ and προφυγόντα ‘having escaped’, an aorist participle of προφεύγω taking μένος ‘might’ and χεῖρας ‘hands’ as objects. The meaning of ἀάπτους is not known; ‘untouchable’ and ‘irresistible’ are two traditional guesses.

sentences.t: καί ῥ’ ἦγον προτὶ ἄστυ ἀελπτέοντες σόον εἶναι.
sentences.l: and they led him toward the town, not hoping that he was safe.
sentences.i: and they led him toward the town, not hoping that he was safe.
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ is καὶ ῥα ‘and then’; ἦγον is the imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead’ and προτί is πρός ‘toward’. ἀελπτέοντες is a present participle of ἀελπτέω ‘be without hope’ (ἀ- ‘not’ + the root of ἐλπίς ‘hope’), and σόον εἶναι is ‘that he was safe’. The participle says the Trojans had given up hope of seeing him safe; the Greek does not say more.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
εἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον ἄγον κεχαρηότα νίκῃ.
sentences.l:
And Ajax, again, from the other side, the well-greaved Achaeans
led to heavenly Agamemnon, rejoicing in victory.
sentences.i: On the other side the well-greaved Achaeans led Ajax, rejoicing in his victory, to heavenly Agamemnon.
sentences.n: The Achaean side is shown in turn. Αἴαντ’ is the elided accusative Αἴαντα, object of ἄγον ‘led’; αὖθ’ is an elided form meaning ‘again, in turn’, and ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ sets this against the Trojans’ scene. ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί ‘well-greaved Achaeans’ and δῖον ‘heavenly’ are stock epithets, translated each time. κεχαρηότα is a perfect participle of χαίρω, ‘rejoicing’, with νίκῃ ‘in victory’: the poet calls it Ajax’s victory although the fight was broken off before either man was beaten.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίῃσιν ἐν Ἀτρεΐδαο γένοντο,
τοῖσι δὲ βοῦν ἱέρευσεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
ἄρσενα πενταέτηρον ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι.
sentences.i: When they reached the huts of the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men, sacrificed for them a male five-year-old ox to the son of Cronus, of surpassing strength.
sentences.n: A new paragraph: the sacrifice that ends the day. οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ … γένοντο is ‘and when they had come to be (in)’, with ἐν Ἀτρεΐδαο κλισίῃσιν ‘in the huts of Atreus’ son’ (κλισίῃσιν is the epic dative plural). The main clause starts at line 2 with τοῖσι δέ ‘for them’, βοῦν ἱέρευσεν ‘sacrificed an ox’, ἄρσενα πενταέτηρον ‘male, five years old’ (πέντε + ἔτος), and ὑπερμενέϊ Κρονίωνι ‘to the son of Cronus of surpassing strength’, Zeus, ὑπερμενής being a stock epithet.

sentences.t:
τὸν δέρον ἀμφί θ’ ἕπον, καί μιν διέχευαν ἅπαντα,
μίστυλλόν τ’ ἄρ’ ἐπισταμένως πεῖράν τ’ ὀβελοῖσιν,
ὄπτησάν τε περιφραδέως, ἐρύσαντό τε πάντα.
sentences.l:
him they flayed and dressed, and cut him up, all of him,
and cut into pieces skilfully and pierced on spits,
and roasted them very carefully and drew them all off.
sentences.i: They flayed it and dressed the carcass, and cut up the whole of it, and cut the meat skilfully into small pieces and pierced them on spits, and roasted them with great care, and drew them all off.
sentences.n: The butchery is told in the order it is done, one verb after another. τὸν is ‘it’, the ox; δέρον is the imperfect of δέρω ‘flay’ with no augment, and ἀμφί … ἕπον a tmesis (split compound) of ἀμφέπω ‘attend to’, which with δέρω is ‘dress’ the carcass. διέχευαν is ‘cut up’ (literally ‘poured apart’), μίστυλλον ‘cut into small pieces’, ἐπισταμένως ‘skilfully’, πεῖραν ‘pierced’ (ἔπειραν without augment), ὀβελοῖσιν ‘on spits’. ὄπτησαν is ‘roasted’ (1.466 has the augmented ὤπτησαν), περιφραδέως ‘very carefully’, and ἐρύσαντο ‘drew off’ the meat from the spits.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ παύσαντο πόνου τετύκοντό τε δαῖτα,
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης·
sentences.l:
And when they had ceased from toil and had made ready the feast,
they feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast.
sentences.i: And when they had ended their labour and prepared the meal, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast.
sentences.n: The meal formula, the same two lines as at 1.467–468. παύσαντο is the aorist middle of παύω ‘cease’, with the genitive πόνου ‘from toil’; τετύκοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of τεύχω, ‘made ready’, with δαῖτα ‘feast’. δαίνυντ’ is the imperfect of δαίνυμι ‘feast’, elided. ἐδεύετο is the imperfect of δεύομαι ‘lack’, with the genitive δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘an equal feast’, equal because each guest’s share is the same.

sentences.t:
νώτοισιν δ’ Αἴαντα διηνεκέεσσι γέραιρεν
ἥρως Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.l:
and with chines unbroken he honoured Ajax,
the hero, Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon.
sentences.i: And the hero Agamemnon, son of Atreus, wide-ruling, honoured Ajax with long unbroken cuts of chine.
sentences.n: Ajax is given the place of honour at the meat. νώτοισιν is the dative plural of νῶτον ‘back’, here the chine, the cuts of meat from along the backbone, and διηνεκέεσσι the epic dative plural of διηνεκής ‘unbroken, continuous’. γέραιρεν is the imperfect of γεραίρω ‘honour’, a verb related to γέρας ‘prize of honour’, and takes Αἴαντα as its object. The subject waits for line 2: ἥρως ‘the hero’, Ἀτρεΐδης, and εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘wide-ruling Agamemnon’ (printed as two words).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
τοῖς ὁ γέρων πάμπρωτος ὑφαίνειν ἤρχετο μῆτιν
Νέστωρ, οὗ καὶ πρόσθεν ἀρίστη φαίνετο βουλή·
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the old man was the first of all to begin weaving a plan for them: Nestor, whose counsel had also seemed best before.
sentences.n: The end of the meal, and Nestor speaks. ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο is the stock phrase ‘put away desire’: ἕντο is the aorist middle of ἵημι, ἔρον the accusative of ἔρος ‘desire’, and ἐξ is cut off from its verb. ὁ γέρων ‘the old man’ is the article as a demonstrative, with the name held back to line 3; πάμπρωτος is ‘first of all’, and ὑφαίνειν μῆτιν ‘to weave a plan’ pictures planning as weaving. οὗ is the relative ‘whose’, and φαίνετο ‘appeared’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The stock introduction to a speech, spoken here by Nestor. ὅ is the article as a pronoun, ‘he’; σφιν is ‘to them’; ἐϋφρονέων, which the edition prints as one word, is a participle of ἐϋφρονέω ‘be well-disposed’. ἀγορήσατο is the aorist of ἀγοράομαι ‘address an assembly’, and μετέειπεν ‘spoke among them’.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν,
πολλοὶ γὰρ τεθνᾶσι κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί,
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, and you other best men of the Achaeans all together,
for many have died, the long-haired-of-head Achaeans,
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, and you other best men of all the Achaeans, for many long-haired Achaeans have died,
sentences.n: Nestor names those he addresses. Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative of Ἀτρεΐδης, Agamemnon; ἄλλοι ἀριστῆες Παναχαιῶν ‘the other best men of the Achaeans all together’ is a nominative used as a vocative. τεθνᾶσι is the perfect of θνῄσκω ‘die’, ‘are dead’. κάρη κομόωντες ‘long-haired-of-head’ is the stock epithet of the Achaeans, always translated. Nestor’s speech begins, and the sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
τῶν νῦν αἷμα κελαινὸν ἐΰρροον ἀμφὶ Σκάμανδρον
ἐσκέδασ’ ὀξὺς Ἄρης, ψυχαὶ δ’ Ἄϊδος δὲ κατῆλθον·
sentences.l:
of whom now the dark blood, around fair-flowing Scamander,
sharp Ares has scattered, and their souls to Hades have gone down;
sentences.i: whose dark blood sharp Ares has now scattered around the fair-flowing Scamander, and their souls have gone down to Hades;
sentences.n: The dead are the reason for what Nestor proposes. τῶν ‘of these’ is the article as a relative, with αἷμα κελαινόν ‘dark blood’. ἐΰρροον ‘fair-flowing’ could in the Greek go with αἷμα or with Σκάμανδρον; the translation takes it with the river. ἐσκέδασ’ is the elided aorist of σκεδάννυμι ‘scatter’, and ὀξὺς Ἄρης ‘sharp Ares’ is the war-god standing for the fighting itself. ψυχαί ‘souls’ are what survives the body; Ἄϊδος δέ, printed as two words, is the genitive Ἄϊδος with the ending -δε ‘to’ (‘to the house of Hades’), and κατῆλθον ‘went down’.

sentences.t:
τώ σε χρὴ πόλεμον μὲν ἅμ’ ἠοῖ παῦσαι Ἀχαιῶν,
αὐτοὶ δ’ ἀγρόμενοι κυκλήσομεν ἐνθάδε νεκροὺς
βουσὶ καὶ ἡμιόνοισιν·
sentences.i: So you must stop the Achaeans’ fighting at first light, and let us ourselves gather and haul the dead here with oxen and mules;
sentences.n: Nestor’s plan has three steps, the first for the morning. τώ is ‘therefore’; χρή takes σε and the infinitive παῦσαι, ‘you must stop’, with πόλεμον … Ἀχαιῶν ‘the Achaeans’ war’ and ἅμ’ ἠοῖ ‘with dawn’. ἀγρόμενοι is an aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω, ‘gathered’. κυκλήσομεν has the ending of ‘we shall’ and is read as ‘let us’, a proposal; it comes from κυκλέω ‘wheel’ (κύκλος ‘circle, wheel’), so the dead are hauled here. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 333.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ κατακήομεν αὐτοὺς
τυτθὸν ἀπὸ πρὸ νεῶν, ὥς κ’ ὀστέα παισὶν ἕκαστος
οἴκαδ’ ἄγῃ ὅτ’ ἂν αὖτε νεώμεθα πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
and then let us burn them
a little way off, in front of the ships, so that the bones for the children each man
may take home, when in turn we go back to the fatherland.
sentences.i: and then let us burn them, a little way off in front of the ships, so that each man may take the bones home for the children, when we go back to our fatherland.
sentences.n: The burning, so that the bones can go home. κατακήομεν is the aorist subjunctive of κατακαίω ‘burn’ with the short vowel, ‘let us burn’, and αὐτούς ‘them’ is the dead. τυτθόν is ‘a little’, ἀπό here an adverb ‘away’, and πρὸ νεῶν ‘in front of the ships’. ὥς κ’ … ἄγῃ is a purpose clause; παισίν is ‘for the children’, understood as the dead men’s children, and ἕκαστος is ‘each man’. ὅτ’ ἂν … νεώμεθα is ‘when we go back’, a subjunctive of νέομαι, with πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘fatherland’.

sentences.t:
τύμβον δ’ ἀμφὶ πυρὴν ἕνα χεύομεν ἐξαγαγόντες
ἄκριτον ἐκ πεδίου·
sentences.l:
and a mound around the pyre, one, let us heap up, leading out,
unsorted, from the plain;
sentences.i: and let us bring them out of the plain and heap up around the pyre one undivided mound;
sentences.n: Step two: one mound for all. τύμβον … ἕνα ‘one mound’ and ἀμφὶ πυρήν ‘around the pyre’; χεύομεν is the aorist subjunctive of χέω ‘pour, heap up’, ‘let us heap’. ἐξαγαγόντες ‘leading out’ has no object in the Greek; the dead are understood. ἄκριτον ‘unsorted, not sorted out’ (l keeps the word’s literal sense; i gives it as ‘undivided’, one mound for all) most likely agrees with τύμβον, though it could also mean ‘without sorting’, and the translation takes it with the mound. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 337.

sentences.t:
ποτὶ δ’ αὐτὸν δείμομεν ὦκα
πύργους ὑψηλοὺς εἶλαρ νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν.
sentences.l:
and against it let us build quickly
high towers, a shelter for the ships and for ourselves.
sentences.i: and let us quickly build high towers against it, a shelter for the ships and for ourselves.
sentences.n: Step three begins: towers, the plan for the Achaean wall that is built later in this book. ποτί is πρός ‘against, beside’, and αὐτόν ‘it’ is the mound. δείμομεν is the aorist subjunctive of δέμω ‘build’, and ὦκα ‘quickly’. πύργους ὑψηλούς is ‘high towers’; εἶλαρ ‘shelter’ stands in apposition to them, with the genitive νηῶν ‘of the ships’ and αὐτῶν ‘of ourselves’. The Greek names only towers here, not a continuous wall.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖσι πύλας ποιήσομεν εὖ ἀραρυίας,
ὄφρα δι’ αὐτάων ἱππηλασίη ὁδὸς εἴη·
sentences.l:
and in them gates let us make, well fitted,
so that through them a horse-driving road may be;
sentences.i: and let us make well-fitted gates in them, so that there may be a road for driving horses through them;
sentences.n: The towers need gates. ἐν δ’ αὐτοῖσι is ‘and in them’ (the towers); ἀραρυίας is the feminine accusative plural of the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, so πύλας … εὖ ἀραρυίας is ‘gates well fitted’. ποιήσομεν is read as ‘let us make’, like κυκλήσομεν above. ὄφρα … εἴη is a purpose clause with the optative of εἰμί, δι’ αὐτάων ‘through them’ is an epic form for the gates, and ἱππηλασίη ὁδός is ‘a road for driving horses’ (ἵππος + ἐλαύνω).

sentences.t:
ἔκτοσθεν δὲ βαθεῖαν ὀρύξομεν ἐγγύθι τάφρον,
ἥ χ’ ἵππον καὶ λαὸν ἐρυκάκοι ἀμφὶς ἐοῦσα,
μή ποτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ πόλεμος Τρώων ἀγερώχων.
sentences.l:
and outside a deep ditch let us dig, close by,
which may hold back horse and people, being round about,
lest ever bear down heavily the war of the lofty Trojans.”
sentences.i: and outside, close by, let us dig a deep ditch, one that will hold back horse and people as it lies all round, so that the war of the lofty Trojans may never bear down heavily.”
sentences.n: The ditch finishes the plan, and Nestor’s speech ends. ἔκτοσθεν is ‘outside’, ὀρύξομεν ‘let us dig’ (read like ποιήσομεν), ἐγγύθι ‘close by’. ἥ χ’ ἵππον καὶ λαὸν ἐρυκάκοι is ‘which would hold back horse and people’, with χ’ for κε, the optative of ἐρύκω in a reduplicated aorist form, and ἵππον a collective singular; ἀμφὶς ἐοῦσα is ‘being all round’. μή ποτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ is ‘lest ever it bear down heavily’. ἀγερώχων ‘lofty’ is the stock epithet of the Trojans, of uncertain meaning.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνησαν βασιλῆες.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all approved, the kings.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all the kings agreed.
sentences.n: The Achaean kings accept the plan. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped and its τ made θ before the rough breathing of οἳ); οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’, the article as a pronoun, and βασιλῆες ‘kings’ stands at the end in apposition to πάντες ‘all’. ἐπῄνησαν is the aorist of ἐπαινέω ‘approve’ (Attic ἐπῄνεσαν). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Τρώων αὖτ’ ἀγορὴ γένετ’ Ἰλίου ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ
δεινὴ τετρηχυῖα, παρὰ Πριάμοιο θύρῃσι·
sentences.l:
Of the Trojans, in turn, an assembly came to be, in the high city of Ilios,
dreadful, in turmoil, beside the doors of Priam;
sentences.i: The Trojans, for their part, held an assembly in the high city of Ilios, a dreadful one, in turmoil, beside the doors of Priam;
sentences.n: The scene moves to Troy. Τρώων … ἀγορή is ‘an assembly of the Trojans’; αὖτ’ ‘in turn’ answers the Achaean council just ended, and γένετ’ (γένετο) ‘came to be’ means ‘was held’. Ἰλίου ἐν πόλει ἄκρῃ is ‘in the high city of Ilios’, the upper town. δεινή ‘dreadful’ and τετρηχυῖα, a perfect participle meaning ‘roughened, in turmoil’ (from the root of τρηχύς ‘rough’), both describe the assembly; παρὰ Πριάμοιο θύρῃσι is ‘beside Priam’s doors’, with θύρῃσι the epic dative plural.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντήνωρ πεπνυμένος ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.l: and among them prudent Antenor began to speak:
sentences.i: Prudent Antenor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: Antenor, one of the Trojan elders, speaks first. τοῖσιν is ‘among them’, the dative plural of the article with the epic ending -σιν; ἦρχ’ (ἦρχε) ἀγορεύειν is ‘began to speak’, the infinitive of ἀγορεύω ‘speak in assembly’. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is his standing epithet.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ Δάρδανοι ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: The opening of a speech to an assembly. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with μευ the genitive ‘me’. Δάρδανοι are the Dardanians, a people allied with the Trojans, and ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ the fighters who came to help Troy. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may say’, and τά με θυμὸς … κελεύει is ‘what my heart bids me’, with θυμός ‘heart’ as the seat of impulse. Priam’s speech opens with the same two lines (368–369).

sentences.t:
δεῦτ’ ἄγετ’ Ἀργείην Ἑλένην καὶ κτήμαθ’ ἅμ’ αὐτῇ
δώομεν Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν ἄγειν·
sentences.l:
Come hither, come, Argive Helen and the possessions with her
let us give to the sons of Atreus to take away;
sentences.i: Come, let us give Argive Helen, and the possessions with her, to the sons of Atreus to take away;
sentences.n: Antenor’s proposal: give her back. δεῦτ’ ἄγετ’ is ‘come here, come on’, a plural call to action. Ἀργείην Ἑλένην is ‘Argive Helen’, and κτήμαθ’ is κτήματα ‘possessions’, the goods that went with her. δώομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive of δίδωμι, ‘let us give’, Ἀτρεΐδῃσιν the dative plural ‘to the sons of Atreus’ (Agamemnon and Menelaus), and ἄγειν ‘to lead away, take away’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 351.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὅρκια πιστὰ
ψευσάμενοι μαχόμεσθα·
sentences.l:
but now, having been false to the faithful oaths,
we are fighting;
sentences.i: but now we are fighting after breaking our faithful oaths;
sentences.n: His reason. νῦν δ’ ‘but now’ sets the present against the proposal. ὅρκια πιστά is ‘faithful oaths’, the truce sworn in Book 3 and broken in Book 4. ψευσάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ψεύδομαι ‘lie, be false’, here with the oaths as object, ‘having been false to’. μαχόμεσθα is the first-person plural ‘we are fighting’ with the epic ending -μεσθα. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 352.

sentences.t:
τὼ οὔ νύ τι κέρδιον ἡμῖν
ἔλπομαι ἐκτελέεσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ῥέξομεν ὧδε.
sentences.l:
therefore not at all anything better for us
I expect to be accomplished, unless we do thus.”
sentences.i: So I do not expect anything better to come about for us, unless we do this.”
sentences.n: His conclusion. τώ is ‘therefore’, as at 331. οὔ νύ τι κέρδιον ἡμῖν ἔλπομαι is ‘I expect nothing better for us’: κέρδιον is ‘better, more to our advantage’, and ἔλπομαι ‘I expect’ (it need not mean hope). ἐκτελέεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to be brought to pass’. ἵνα μὴ ῥέξομεν ὧδε is awkward: ἵνα with μή would usually mean ‘so that we may not’, but the sense needed is ‘unless we do so’, with ὧδε ‘thus’ and ῥέξομεν from ῥέζω ‘do’. Antenor’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο· τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
δῖος Ἀλέξανδρος Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο,
ὅς μιν ἀμειβόμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
He then, having so spoken, sat down; and among them stood up
heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
who, answering him, winged words spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down; and among them there stood up heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen, who in answer to him spoke winged words:
sentences.n: Paris answers Antenor. ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο is the stock phrase for a speaker sitting down (κατά is cut off from its verb), and τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη ‘and among them stood up’. Alexander is the other name of Paris, δῖος ‘heavenly’ is his stock epithet, and Ἑλένης πόσις ἠϋκόμοιο is ‘husband of fine-haired Helen’, the woman Antenor has just proposed to give up. ὅς μιν ἀμειβόμενος: ὅς is ‘who’, μιν is Antenor, and ἀμειβόμενος ‘answering’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the stock phrase. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
Ἀντῆνορ σὺ μὲν οὐκέτ’ ἐμοὶ φίλα ταῦτ’ ἀγορεύεις·
οἶσθα καὶ ἄλλον μῦθον ἀμείνονα τοῦδε νοῆσαι.
sentences.l:
“Antenor, you no longer say things dear to me;
you know how to devise also another speech, better than this.
sentences.i: “Antenor, what you are saying is no longer dear to me; you know how to think of a better thing to say than this.
sentences.n: Paris rejects it. Ἀντῆνορ is the vocative of Ἀντήνωρ, with the short ο of the stem in place of the nominative’s ω. σὺ μέν ‘you, for your part’ has no matching δέ. οὐκέτ’ ἐμοὶ φίλα is ‘no longer dear to me’ (οὐκέτι ‘no longer’). οἶσθα … νοῆσαι is ‘you know how to devise’, with οἶσθα from οἶδα ‘know’ and the infinitive of νοέω ‘think of’; ἄλλον μῦθον ἀμείνονα τοῦδε is ‘another speech better than this one’, with τοῦδε a genitive of comparison.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν δὴ τοῦτον ἀπὸ σπουδῆς ἀγορεύεις,
ἐξ ἄρα δή τοι ἔπειτα θεοὶ φρένας ὤλεσαν αὐτοί.
sentences.l:
But if truly indeed this you say in earnest,
then the gods themselves have utterly destroyed your wits.
sentences.i: But if you really are saying this in earnest, then the gods themselves have destroyed your wits.
sentences.n: He turns the proposal into an insult. εἰ δ’ ἐτεὸν δή is ‘but if truly indeed’, with ἐτεόν the neuter of ἐτεός used as an adverb; τοῦτον is the proposal, and ἀπὸ σπουδῆς is ‘in earnest’ (σπουδή ‘seriousness’). The main clause is ἐξ … ὤλεσαν, a split compound of ἐξόλλυμι ‘destroy utterly’, with θεοὶ … αὐτοί ‘the gods themselves’, τοι for σοι ‘your’, and φρένας ‘wits’. The aorist states the conclusion as a fact: if he means it, the harm is already done.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ Τρώεσσι μεθ’ ἱπποδάμοις ἀγορεύσω·
sentences.l: But I shall speak among the horse-taming Trojans;
sentences.i: But I shall speak among the Trojans, tamers of horses;
sentences.n: Paris will make his own proposal to the assembly. αὐτὰρ ἐγώ ‘but I’; ἀγορεύσω ‘I shall speak’; μεθ’ is μετά ‘among’, with the dative Τρώεσσι in the epic ending -εσσι. ἱπποδάμοις ‘horse-taming’ is the stock epithet of the Trojans, translated each time. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἀπόφημι γυναῖκα μὲν οὐκ ἀποδώσω·
sentences.l: and straight out I declare: the woman, for one, I will not give back;
sentences.i: and I say it outright: the woman I shall not give back;
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ is ‘straight out, outright’. ἀπόφημι is ‘I declare’ (the verb can also mean ‘deny, refuse’, and what follows is a refusal), and it introduces the clause with no conjunction. γυναῖκα is ‘woman’, Helen unnamed; μέν is answered by κτήματα δέ in the next line, the woman on one side and the goods on the other. ἀποδώσω is the future of ἀποδίδωμι ‘give back’, with οὐκ.

sentences.t:
κτήματα δ’ ὅσσ’ ἀγόμην ἐξ Ἄργεος ἡμέτερον δῶ
πάντ’ ἐθέλω δόμεναι καὶ οἴκοθεν ἄλλ’ ἐπιθεῖναι.
sentences.l:
but the possessions, as many as I brought from Argos to our house,
all I am willing to give, and to add others from my own house.”
sentences.i: but all the possessions that I brought from Argos to our house I am willing to give, and to add others from my own house besides.”
sentences.n: He gives up only the goods. κτήματα δ’ answers γυναῖκα μέν above. ὅσσ’ ἀγόμην is ‘as many as I brought’, ἀγόμην an imperfect middle of ἄγω, ‘led with me’; ἐξ Ἄργεος is ‘from Argos’, the Achaean land (compare Ἀργείη Ἑλένη). ἡμέτερον δῶ is ‘to our house’, with δῶ the short form of δῶμα. πάντ’ ἐθέλω δόμεναι is ‘I am willing to give all’, δόμεναι the epic infinitive of δίδωμι, and οἴκοθεν ἄλλ’ ἐπιθεῖναι ‘to add other things from home’, an aorist infinitive of ἐπιτίθημι. Alexander’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο· τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος, θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος,
sentences.l:
He then, having so spoken, sat down; and among them stood up
Dardanus’ descendant Priam, a counsellor equal to the gods,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down; and among them there stood up Priam, a descendant of Dardanus, a counsellor equal to the gods,
sentences.n: Priam rises, with the same sitting-down formula as at 354. Δαρδανίδης Πρίαμος is ‘Priam, descendant of Dardanus’: the ending -ίδης marks descent, not necessarily a son. θεόφιν μήστωρ ἀτάλαντος is ‘a counsellor equal to the gods’: θεόφιν has the old ending -φιν (‘to, with the gods’), μήστωρ is ‘counsellor, planner’, and ἀτάλαντος ‘equal’ (literally ‘equal in weight’). A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐϋφρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: The same stock introduction as at 326, now of Priam; μετέειπε here lacks the final -ν of μετέειπεν there, with no change of sense. ὅ is the article as a pronoun, ‘he’; σφιν ‘to them’; ἐϋφρονέων a participle of ἐϋφρονέω ‘be well-disposed’; ἀγορήσατο the aorist of ἀγοράομαι ‘address an assembly’.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ Τρῶες καὶ Δάρδανοι ἠδ’ ἐπίκουροι,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, Trojans and Dardanians and allies,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, Trojans, Dardanians and allies, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Priam opens with the same two lines as Antenor (348–349). κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with μευ ‘me’; Δάρδανοι are the Dardanians and ἐπίκουροι ‘allies’ the fighters who came to help Troy. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause, ‘so that I may say’, and τά με θυμὸς … κελεύει ‘what my heart bids me’. Priam’s speech begins.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δόρπον ἕλεσθε κατὰ πτόλιν ὡς τὸ πάρος περ,
καὶ φυλακῆς μνήσασθε καὶ ἐγρήγορθε ἕκαστος·
sentences.l:
Now take your supper through the city, as before,
and be mindful of the watch, and be wakeful, each one;
sentences.i: For now, take your supper through the city as before, and be mindful of the watch, and keep awake, each one of you;
sentences.n: Priam’s orders for the night. νῦν μέν ‘for now’ looks forward to ἠῶθεν δέ ‘at dawn’ in the next unit. δόρπον ἕλεσθε is ‘take your supper’ (ἕλεσθε is the aorist middle imperative of αἱρέω), κατὰ πτόλιν ‘through the city’ (πτόλις is πόλις), and ὡς τὸ πάρος περ ‘just as before’. φυλακῆς μνήσασθε is ‘think of the watch’, with the genitive; ἐγρήγορθε is the perfect imperative of ἐγείρω, ‘be awake’, and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is singular after a plural command.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δ’ Ἰδαῖος ἴτω κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας
εἰπέμεν Ἀτρεΐδῃς Ἀγαμέμνονι καὶ Μενελάῳ
μῦθον Ἀλεξάνδροιο, τοῦ εἵνεκα νεῖκος ὄρωρε·
sentences.i: and at dawn let Idaeus go to the hollow ships to tell the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, the word of Alexander, for whose sake the quarrel has arisen;
sentences.n: Priam sends Idaeus, the Trojan herald who stopped the duel in the previous part. ἠῶθεν is ‘at dawn’ and ἴτω the third-person imperative of εἶμι, ‘let him go’. εἰπέμεν is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to tell’; Ἀτρεΐδῃς is the dative plural ‘to the sons of Atreus’, with the two names in apposition. μῦθον Ἀλεξάνδροιο is ‘the word of Alexander’, the offer just made. τοῦ εἵνεκα νεῖκος ὄρωρε is ‘on whose account the quarrel has arisen’, with ὄρωρε the perfect of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, used intransitively.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ τόδ’ εἰπέμεναι πυκινὸν ἔπος, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωσι
παύσασθαι πολέμοιο δυσηχέος, εἰς ὅ κε νεκροὺς
κήομεν· ὕστερον αὖτε μαχησόμεθ’ εἰς ὅ κε δαίμων
ἄμμε διακρίνῃ, δώῃ δ’ ἑτέροισί γε νίκην.
sentences.l:
and this too to say, a shrewd word, if they are willing
to cease from ill-sounding war, until the dead
we burn; later in turn we shall fight, until a divinity
parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.”
sentences.i: and to say this too, a shrewd word, if they are willing to cease from ill-sounding war until we burn the dead; later we shall fight again, until a divinity parts us and gives victory to one side or the other.”
sentences.n: A second message, asking for a truce to burn the dead. καὶ δέ is ‘and also’, τόδε ‘this’ looks ahead, and εἰπέμεναι is a second infinitive after ἴτω; πυκινὸν ἔπος is ‘a shrewd word’ (πυκινός ‘close-packed, shrewd’). αἴ κ’ ἐθέλωσι is ‘if they are willing’, with παύσασθαι governing the genitive πολέμοιο δυσηχέος ‘ill-sounding war’ (δυσ- ‘ill’ + ἦχος ‘sound’). εἰς ὅ κε … κήομεν is ‘until we burn’, a short-vowel subjunctive of καίω. The last two lines are word for word Hector’s at 291–292. Priam’s speech ends here.
